desc:
A network has n servers numbered 0 to n - 1. Each entry links[i] = [a, b, q] is a two-way link between servers a and b that lets only one packet in every q through, so a packet crosses it with probability 1/q. A link with q = 1 never loses anything. Several links may join the same pair of servers.

A route is a chain of links from src to dst. Crossing all its links in turn succeeds with probability 1 / (q1 · q2 · ...), so we call q1 · q2 · ... the loss factor of the route (the empty route from a server to itself has loss factor 1). Return the smallest loss factor over all routes from src to dst, which is the most reliable route, or -1 if the two servers are not connected.

The input guarantees that when dst is reachable, the smallest loss factor is at most 231 - 1. Loss factors of other, worse routes may be larger.

n = 4, src = 0, dst = 3
links = [[0,1,2], [1,3,2], [0,3,5], [0,2,1], [2,3,3]]
0-1-3: 2*2 = 4,  0-3: 5,  0-2-3: 1*3 = 3
-> 3
constraints: If dst is reachable, the smallest loss factor is at most 2<sup>31</sup> - 1
hints: Probabilities multiply along a route, so the best route is the one with the smallest product of the q values, not the one with the fewest links.
Dijkstra only needs one property of the route cost: it never decreases when you extend the route. Is that true for a product of numbers that are all at least 1?
Run Dijkstra with 'cost' = product of q instead of sum. Start with product 1 at src, relax with nd = d * q, and skip any product above 231 - 1 (it can never be the answer, and it avoids overflow).
editorial: Dijkstra's algorithm works for any cost that is built from the route with an operation that never makes the cost smaller. Here the cost is a product of factors that are all at least 1, so extending a route never decreases it, and the first time a server is popped from the min-heap its product is final. The only changes from the textbook version are that the start has cost 1 (the empty product) and that relaxation multiplies instead of adding.

The input guarantees the optimal product fits in 32 bits, so any candidate larger than 231 - 1 can be dropped. This prevents overflow in fixed-width languages and is safe: a route whose product already exceeds the bound can only grow, so it cannot lead to the optimum. If dst never gets popped, return -1.

A second way to see it is to take logarithms: maximising probability means minimising the sum of log q, an ordinary non-negative shortest path. Working with exact integer products avoids floating-point error. Time O((V + E) log E).
